MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF THE PENNSYLVANIA 
OFFICE OF CONSUMER ADVOCATE 
 
 
The Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate (PA OCA) moves for leave to answer 
(Motion) and submits this Answer1 in support of the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition and the 
Industrial Energy Consumers of America’s (collectively, ICC) Request for Clarification or 
Rehearing (ICC’s Request) filed on January 20, 2026, to the Commission’s December 18 Order 
issued in the above-captioned docket (Order). Good cause exists for the Commission to accept this 
Answer because it contributes an end-use consumer voice2 to the Commission’s decision-making 
to clarify the Order according to its consumer-protective intent regarding behind-the-meter 
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213 (listing Commission rules for Motions and Answers; Section 385.212(a)(2) 
provides that “[a]n answer may not be made to . . . a request for rehearing, unless otherwise ordered by the 
decisional authority.”); Alaska Gasline Dev. Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,134, at P 7 (2020) (accepting answers that 
“clarify the concerns raised and provide information that has assisted in [the Commission’s] decision making”). 
2 See Xcel Energy Services, Inc. v. FERC, 815 F.3d 947, 952 (D.C. Cir. 2016) (“It is long-established that the ‘primary 
aim [of the FPA] is the protection of consumers from excessive rates and charges.’” (quoting Mun. Light Bds. Of 
Reading & Wakefield v. FPC, 450 F.2d 1341, 1348 (D.C. Cir. 1971))); Nat’l Ass’n of Regulatory Util. Comm’rs v. 
FERC, 964 F.3d 1177, 1186 (D.C. Cir. 2020) (noting FPA’s “‘core purposes’ of ‘curb[ing] prices and enhanc[ing] 
reliability in the wholesale electricity market’” (quoting FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 273 
(2016))).

2 
 
generation (BTMG) and co-located load.3 In support of the ICC’s Request, because the proceeding 
did not develop a legally sufficient record on BTMG, FERC and PJM should approach BTMG by 
continuing to focus where FERC and PJM have been focusing: on “the scale of large data centers” 
and “very large loads like data centers” trying to evade or manipulate the Co-Location rules in 
ways that create a “potential transmission and resource adequacy planning problem” and “raise 
cost shifting concerns.”4  
I. 
Summary of Answer to the ICC’s Request 
For context, in Pennsylvania, certain existing industrial customers have invested 
significantly in combined heat and power (CHP) cogeneration facilities that support their 
manufacturing processes and offset their electricity consumption. The cogeneration facilities 
generate combined electrical and thermal energy. Thermal energy, or heat, is used in the 
manufacturing process and the electricity byproduct is used to power their business. These CHP 
cogeneration facilities are BTMG, are not used in PJM’s energy or capacity markets, and do not 
use the PJM transmission system because when the generation trips offline, the load connected to 
the BTMG (or almost all of the load) automatically trips offline. Such a configuration ensures that 
the load with BTMG does not materially “lean” on PJM.5 
In addressing PJM’s BTMG rule, FERC should adhere to the jurisdictional limits expressed 
in the Order to preserve exclusive state retail authority and protect consumers from cost shifts, 
because doing so will improve the Order’s legal durability and effectuate its purpose. Furthermore, 
FERC should evaluate whether and how to set an appropriate threshold(s) with continued attention 
to the distinction between unique new large loads—primarily data center large loads—and existing 
 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 186 (2025) (December 18 Order) (expressing consumer-
protective intent).  
4 Id. (quoting PJM March 24 Response at 13, 36). 
5 See ICC’s Request, at pp. 28, 32 (identifying potential effects on Combined Heat and Power Units).

3 
 
BTMG facilities, like Pennsylvania industrial consumers with CHP cogeneration facilities, that 
FERC explicitly sought to protect through the threshold. Alternatively, a qualitative distinction 
based on reliability implications can be used to separate existing BTMG facilities within PJM from 
data center large loads because the existing CHP cogeneration facilities in Pennsylvania, for 
example, do not use PJM’s energy or capacity markets and do not use the PJM transmission system, 
and these particular qualities could be a way to ensure appropriate treatment of these existing CHG 
cogeneration facilities.  Throughout this proceeding, the Commission should continue its vital 
focus on addressing new data center large load configurations that shift costs and create 
transmission and resource adequacy planning problems. 
II. 
Background on the Order’s BTMG Provisions 
In the Order, the Commission found PJM’s existing BTMG rules to be no longer just and 
reasonable because “loads with BTMG are not fully accounted for in resource adequacy planning,” 
which creates a “potential transmission and resource adequacy planning problem” and “raise[s] 
cost shifting concerns.”6 FERC reasoned that the existing rules may present “both reliability and 
resource adequacy risks because PJM, per its Tariff, is obligated to serve transmission customers 
using BTMG but does not consider such customers in transmission and resource adequacy 
planning.”7 On that basis, FERC directed “PJM to revise its BTMG rules.”8  
In recognition of “concerns raised in the record about the potential impacts on existing 
BTMG customers of the Commission changing PJM’s BTMG rules, however, [the Commission] 
direct[ed] PJM to maintain the current BTMG rules for customers that fall below a new [megawatt] 
[(MW)] materiality threshold for the amount of load at a particular electrical location that Network 
 
6 December 18 Order, at PP 179, 186. 
7 Id. at 179. 
8 Id.

4 
 
Customers may net using BTMG.”9 Furthermore, FERC directed  “PJM to implement a two-part 
transition process for retail BTMG . . . including: (1) the establishment of a three-year transition 
period; and (2) the ability to grandfather certain entities with existing contracts . . . .”10 
In making these decisions, FERC noted that “PJM explains that the BTMG rules were 
‘conceived for, and [have] been implemented for, substantially smaller loads (like a warehouse 
with solar panels) and not on the scale of large data centers.’”11 Moreover, FERC identified that 
“PJM’s existing BTMG rules do not limit the amount of qualifying load that a Network Customer 
may net by using BTMG and do not provide any protections against this potential transmission 
and resource adequacy planning problem or against the costs of maintaining sufficient resources 
to serve these loads being shifted onto other customers.”12 For these reasons, FERC determined 
that large load BTMG arrangements violate cost causation principles because “large loads 
configured in a BTMG arrangement with significant generation will raise cost shifting concerns 
compared to loads pursuing smaller amounts of netting.”13 FERC applied this finding that the PJM 
Tariff’s BTMG provisions are unjust and unreasonable “to all Network Load.”14 
In directing PJM’s Tariff revisions, FERC carefully noted that “not all loads using BTMG 
are large loads that create the reliability and resource adequacy risks” that caused FERC’s finding.15 
FERC posited that electricity output in MW is an essential variable in distinguishing BTMG that 
creates reliability and resource adequacy risks from BTMG that does not. On this basis, FERC 
directed PJM “to propose a new MW threshold for the amount of load at a particular electrical 
 
9 Id. 
10 Id. 
11 December 18 Order, at P 186. 
12 Id. at P 186 (citing PJM, Intra-PJM Tariffs, OATT, § III.34.2 Netting of Behind the Meter Generation (0.0.0)). 
13 Id. 
14 Id. 
15 Id. at P 221.

5 
 
location that Network Customers may net by using BTMG.”16 The threshold seeks to “reduce the 
reliability and resource adequacy risks” from large loads identified in the Order “while also 
allowing for Network Customers to reduce their transmission charges in a transparent, not unduly 
discriminatory fashion.”17 
FERC’s BTMG determination concerns only retail BTMG, not non-retail BTMG.18 “PJM 
defines Non-Retail BTMG as BTMG that is ‘used by municipal electric systems, electric 
cooperatives, or electric distribution companies to serve load.’”19 FERC defined Co-Located Load, 
the true focus of the Order, as “a configuration that refers to end-use customer load that is 
physically connected to the facilities of an existing or planned Customer Facility on the 
Interconnection Customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection to the PJM Transmission 
System.”20 In adopting this definition, FERC limited the Order’s jurisdictional scope to 
“jurisdiction to oversee the interconnection of generating facilities, including the generators that 
are used to serve Co-Located Load, to the interstate transmission system, as well as jurisdiction 
over the provision of transmission service in interstate commerce used by an Eligible Customer to 
serve Co-Located Load.”21 FERC framed this discussion in terms of its statutorily limited 
jurisdictional role in the federalist system,22 highlighting “that the FPA’s jurisdictional divide ‘was 
 
16 December 18 Order, at P 221. 
17 Id. 
18 Id. at P 222. 
19 Id. at P 222 n. 456 (quoting PJM, Intra-PJM Tariffs, OATT, § I.1 Definitions – L-M-N (51.0.1) (defining Non-
Retail BTMG)), 
20 Id. at P 164 (citation omitted). “PJM defines Interconnection Customer as a Generation Interconnection Customer 
and/or a Transmission Interconnection Customer.” Id. at P 2 n.5 (citing PJM, Intra-PJM Tariffs, OATT, § I.1 
Definitions – I – J - K (15.0.0)). 
21 December 18 Order, at P 170. 
22 Id. at P 166.

6 
 
drawn with meticulous regard for the continued exercise of state power, not to handicap or dilute 
it in any way.’”23 
III. 
FERC Should Adhere to the Jurisdictional Limits Expressed in the Order to Preserve 
Exclusive State Retail Authority and Protect Consumers from Cost Shifts, Because Doing So 
Will Improve the Order’s Legal Durability and Effectuate Its Purpose. 
 
The ICC’s Request correctly notes that “the Order does not sufficiently explain the legal 
basis for asserting jurisdiction over retail customers with [BTMG] that is not otherwise used in 
PJM’s energy or capacity markets and does not use the PJM transmission system.”24 In accordance 
with FERC’s jurisdictional analysis in the Order, the ICC identifies that “any regulations the 
Commission fashions must be based on its statutory authority over interstate transmission and 
wholesale sales.”25 
In evaluating PJM’s tariff revisions, FERC should ensure that PJM has clarified exactly 
how it interprets the definitions of BTMG and Co-Located Load, especially in relation to 
jurisdiction. The Order “clarif[ied] that, consistent with the definition in 159, provided above, 
supra P 164, BTMG is not Co-Located Load.”26 But the exact relationship between them remains 
unclear. 
FERC should ensure that PJM’s Tariff reaffirms and clearly demarcates distinctions 
between (1) retail BTMG, (2) retail BTMG that directly affects interstate transmission or interstate 
wholesale sales but retains an exclusively state-jurisdictional retail component, and (3) the FERC-
jurisdictional aspects of Co-Located Load configurations—which FERC carefully explained are 
 
23 Id. (quoting Oneok, Inc. v. Learjet, Inc., 575 U.S. 373, 384-85 (2015) (discussing the analogous provisions in the 
Natural Gas Act) (quoting Panhandle E. Pipe Line Co. v. Pub. Serv. Comm’n of Ind., 332 U.S. 507, 517-18 (1947))). 
24 ICC Request, at p. 21. 
25 Compare ICC Request at p. 39 with December 18 Order, at P 166 (identifying FERC’s statutory limits). 
26 December 18 Order, at P 221 n.453.

7 
 
its wholesale generator interconnection and interstate transmission aspects. These are three distinct 
categories. 
(1) Retail BTMG under PJM’s existing Tariff is, by definition, exclusively state 
jurisdictional and therefore outside the scope of federal jurisdiction, including outside FERC’s 
jurisdiction in the Co-Location Order.27 
(2) Assuming that FERC has asserted jurisdiction over a narrow class of retail BTMG 
related to “very large loads like data centers,”28 or some interstate transmission aspect of a larger 
class of retail BTMG, that jurisdiction would be valid only to the extent that it preserves states’ 
exclusive jurisdiction over retail sales and all other reserved state authority under the Federal 
Power Act.29  An overly broad reading of FERC’s assertion would appear to extend beyond the 
record and the scope of the proceeding on Co-Location. Because the proceeding did not develop a 
legally sufficient record on BTMG, PJM should continue to focus where PJM and FERC have 
been focusing: on “the scale of large data centers” and “very large loads like data centers” that 
“raise cost shifting concerns” by trying to evade or manipulate the Co-Location rules.30 
(3) FERC defined Co-Located Load as “a configuration that refers to end-use customer 
load that is physically connected to the facilities of an existing or planned Customer Facility on 
the Interconnection Customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection to the PJM Transmission 
System.”31 In adopting this definition, FERC limited the Order’s jurisdictional scope to 
“jurisdiction to oversee the interconnection of generating facilities, including the generators that 
 
27 See ICC Request at pp. 40-42 (noting potential jurisdictional confusion); PJM Tariff, Section 1 (Definitions). 
28 December 18 Order, at P 186 (citation omitted). 
29 Id. at PP 165-170; see also Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System, Joint Comments 
of the Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate and Delaware Division of the Public Advocate, at pp. 5-16, Docket 
No. RM26-4-000 (November 21, 2025) (commenting on large load jurisdiction); Tri-State Generation and 
Transmission Ass’n, Inc., 193 FERC ¶ 61,070, at PP 45-50 (2025) (discussing jurisdiction and states’ exclusive retail 
authority). 
30 December 18 Order, at P 186 (citations omitted). 
31 Id. at P 164 (citation omitted).

8 
 
are used to serve Co-Located Load, to the interstate transmission system, as well as jurisdiction 
over the provision of transmission service in interstate commerce used by an Eligible Customer to 
serve Co-Located Load.”32 FERC should ensure that PJM clarifies which, if any, configurations 
under this definition may implement BTMG as a source of generation distinct from the 
Interconnection Customer, with a continued focus on “the scale of large data centers” and “very 
large loads like data centers” that create “potential transmission and resource adequacy planning 
problem” and “raise cost shifting concerns.”33 
IV. 
FERC Should Evaluate Whether and How to Set a MW Threshold(s) with Continued 
Attention to the Distinction Between New Large Loads—Primarily data center large loads—
and Existing BTMG Facilities. 
 
In determining the threshold for load being served by BTMG, FERC should keep in mind 
its choice to highlight PJM’s comments expressing concern specifically about “the scale of large 
data centers.”34 The Commission remarked that “PJM has persuasively explained the problems that 
could occur if Network Customers with large loads were allowed to use the existing BTMG rules 
in the Tariff. For example, PJM explains that ‘[a]llowing very large loads like data centers to net 
is problematic because loads in this configuration do not carry reserves.’”35 
PJM did not support “PJM option 3,” a configuration in which Network Load may Co-
Locate and use BTMG to engage in netting, because “historically, BTMG has supported relatively 
small loads, not on the scale of large data centers.”36  Furthermore, PJM commented that “charging 
load for its net use of the grid under the BTMG rules may not capture the costs caused by co-
 
32 Id. at P 170. 
33 Id. at P 186 (citations omitted). 
34 Id. at P 186 (quoting PJM March 24 Response at 13). 
35 December 18 Order, at P 186 (citations omitted). 
36 Id. at P 16 (citation omitted).

9 
 
located data center arrangements because such arrangements could avoid all costs by netting to 
zero if the entire data center load is supplied by the associated generator.”37 
FERC framed its discussion of BTMG in these terms, sharing PJM’s clear focus on “the 
scale of large data centers.”38 FERC stated “that, while the order is limited to Co-Located Loads, 
this finding [that PJM’s existing BTMG rules may lead to both reliability and resource adequacy 
risks because PJM, per its Tariff, is obligated to serve transmission customers using BTMG but 
does not consider such customers in transmission and resource adequacy planning] applies to all 
Network Load.”39 But an overly broad reading of this assertion would appear to extend beyond the 
record and the scope of the proceeding on Co-Location. Because the proceeding has not yet 
developed a legally sufficient record on BTMG, FERC and PJM should approach the threshold by 
continuing to focus where FERC and PJM have been focusing: on “the scale of large data centers” 
and “very large loads like data centers” that “raise cost shifting concerns” and create “potential 
transmission and resource adequacy planning problem[s].”40 
Moreover, due to the clear focus on new large load configurations—primarily new large 
data center large loads—FERC and PJM should consider whether the load threshold should be 
different and higher for existing BTMG configurations and lower for new BTMG configurations. 
While this would be correctly categorized as “discriminatory,” the Federal Power Act only 
prohibits a “rate, charge, classification, rule, regulation, practice, or contract” that is “unduly 
discriminatory.”41 The best, most natural reading of the plain text is that Congress, by modifying 
“discriminatory” with the word “unduly,” acknowledged the need to duly discriminate when 
 
37 Id. 
38 Id. at P 186 (quoting PJM March 24 Response at 13). 
39 Id. 
40 December 18 Order, at P 186. 
41 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a).

10 
 
appropriate.42 New large loads—primarily data center large loads—have unique effects on the grid 
at a unique time for the PJM market that requires due discrimination to ensure that their integration 
does harm consumers and other grid users.43 
The White House National Energy Dominance Council and a bipartisan group of all 
thirteen Governors of the PJM states have jointly expressed that “today’s data centers [are] 
unique.”44 Specifically, they jointly asserted that the “size and the risks they pose to resource 
adequacy make today’s data centers unique.”45 Moreover, the PJM Independent Market Monitor 
(IMM) has asserted that “the PJM Capacity Market is currently actually significantly short as a 
result of data center load.”46 These statements from the White House, all thirteen bipartisan PJM 
governors, the IMM, and consumer advocates support the notion that “cost shifting concerns” and 
“potential transmission and resource adequacy planning problem[s]” due to the unique challenges 
associated with large data center loads justify treating those challenges on the unique terms that 
they pose to the overall system.47 
FERC, in the Order, made such a due discrimination about large data center loads. Because 
of the “concerns raised in the record about the potential impacts on existing BTMG customers of 
the Commission changing PJM’s BTMG rules, . . . [the Commission] direct[ed] PJM to maintain 
the current BTMG rules for customers that fall below a new MW materiality threshold for the 
 
42 Cf. ANTONIN SCALIA & BRYAN A. GARNER, READING LAW: THE INTERPRETATION OF LEGAL TEXTS 107-08 (2012) 
(explaining expressio unius est exclusio alterius, the negative-implication canon of statutory interpretation). 
43 Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System, Reply Comments of the Pennsylvania Office 
of Consumer Advocate, Delaware Division of the Public Advocate, and People of the State of Illinois by the Office of 
the Illinois Attorney General, at pp. 8-11, Docket No. RM26-4-000 (Dec. 5, 2025). 
44 Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, (Jan. 16, 2026), https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-
regarding-pjm. 
45 Id. 
46 IMM Answer to CEG, at p. 6 (first citing Analysis of the 2026/2027 RPM Base Residual Auction–Part A, 
MONITORING ANALYTICS (Oct., 1, 2025), https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/reports/Reports/2025.shtml; and then 
citing Analysis of the 2027/2028 RPM Base Residual Auction – Part A, MONITORING ANALYTICS (Jan. 5, 2026), 
https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/reports/Reports/2026.shtml). 
47 See December 18 Order, at P 186. As an aside, the Commission should regard with serious skepticism efforts to 
remove existing capacity from the PJM market to serve new data centers. See IMM Answer to CEG, at p. 6.

11 
 
amount of load at a particular electrical location that Network Customers may net using BTMG.”48 
The threshold’s primary purpose is to protect “existing BTMG customers.”49 
FERC should continue to effectuate this intent by ensuring that new rules for BTMG due 
to this unique situation do not unjustly harm other grid users and consumers. For example, BTMG 
units that are CHP cogeneration facilities are longstanding facilities whose operations may be 
severely disrupted if required to fundamentally change how they supply and procure electricity. 
Furthermore, some existing BTMGs that have CHP cogeneration facilities are configured such that 
when the generation trips offline, the load connected to the BTMG (or almost all of the load) 
automatically trips offline. Such a configuration ensures that the load with BTMG does not 
materially “lean” on PJM. 50 Additionally, a Qualifying Facility (QF) under the Public Utility 
Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 (PURPA) occupies particular statutory and regulatory terrain that 
may merit distinct consideration.51 For CHP cogeneration facilities and QFs, especially, FERC 
should ensure that PJM’s selection of threshold(s) is accompanied by analysis regarding the 
threshold’s reliability implications to PJM from disrupting these existing arrangements. Indeed, a 
qualitative distinction based on reliability implications can be used to separate existing BTMG 
facilities within PJM from data center large loads because the existing CHP cogeneration facilities 
in Pennsylvania, for example, do not use PJM’s energy or capacity markets and do not use the PJM 
transmission system, and these particular qualities could be a way to ensure appropriate treatment 
of these existing CHG cogeneration facilities.   
And in general, FERC should ensure that PJM accompanies its selection of threshold(s) 
with analyses regarding the thresholds’ reliability—including operational reliability and resource 
 
48 Id. 
49 Id. 
50 See ICC Request, at pp. 28, 32 (identifying potential effects on Combined Heat and Power Units). 
51 See ICC Request, at pp. 5-6, 10-13 (addressing the unique situation of PURPA QFs).

12 
 
adequacy—implications to PJM and the number of BTMG facilities that are above the 
threshold(s). This information would help stakeholders to assess the threshold(s) and help to avoid 
extensive interconnection studies and other interference with existing BTMG that offer little 
improvement to the Order’s goals of clarifying permissible Co-Located Load configurations and 
addressing “cost shifting concerns” and “potential transmission and resource adequacy planning 
problem[s]” due to large loads that should configure as Co-Located Loads manipulating BTMG to 
avoid paying their fair share of overall system costs.52 
V. 
Conclusion 
The PA OCA respectfully requests that the Commission accept this Answer in support of 
the ICC’s Request because it should assist the Commission in determining appropriate, end-use-
consumer-protective BTMG rules in PJM.
